pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of how the company's work flows through this workspace. Share it with the scheduler, the office manager and every team lead.
What lives where
Clients
: every home, with frequency, bedrooms, bathrooms, entry method, pets and home notes, plus what they owe, how many cleans are booked, and their average rating.
Cleans
: every visit, with the team lead and team, date, price, supplies cost, team hours, margin and the client's rating.
Supplies
: chemicals, cloths and tools, and what to reorder.
Invoices
: monthly bills for recurring clients and one-time cleans.
A clean from booking to paid
New clients start as
New request
. The scheduler sets the date, team lead and team, and moves it to
Scheduled
. A team lead can press
Assign to me
Before leaving, the team reads the client's home notes.
After the clean,
Mark done
stamps the date. The team enters team hours.
The next day the office collects a rating and puts it on the clean.
Recurring clients are billed monthly; one-time cleans the same day. Past due becomes
Overdue
, and Awaiting payment counts sent and overdue.
Mark paid
stamps the date.
Your rhythm
Every morning: Dashboard, today's cleans, overdue invoices
Every afternoon: confirm tomorrow with clients by text
Every Friday: count supplies and check kits
Every month: ratings by team, re-cleans, and recurring bills
Making it yours
Rename teams and clean types, add your own prices, and delete the sample clients once a dozen of your own are in. Type in any cell or drag cards between columns; every total updates by itself.
Keys and codes

Entry details are the most sensitive thing you hold. Keys on file are tagged with a number, never the client's name or address. Door and alarm codes are sent to the team lead by text on the day and are not written on the card. When a client leaves, return their key and note it.
This week at a glance: cleans by status, earnings by type and unpaid invoices.
Overdue cleans
My cleans
Overdue invoices
Awaiting payment (sent and overdue)
Re-cleans requested
Ratings by team
The first clean takes longer than any clean after it, and it decides whether the client stays. Set expectations on the phone, take more time than you think, and write down everything about the home.
On the phone
Ask bedrooms, bathrooms, square footage, pets, and when it was last professionally cleaned. Fill in
Bedrooms
Bathrooms
and
Pets
on the client card.
Ask how the team gets in: client home, lockbox, door code, key on file or garage code. Set
Entry
. Codes go by text, never in writing on the card.
Ask about products: allergies, fragrance-free, natural stone, wood floors, stainless steel.
Price the first clean as a deep clean. Explain that recurring visits cost less because the home is kept up.
What a first clean covers
Kitchen: counters, backsplash, cabinet fronts, appliance fronts, inside the microwave, sink polished
Bathrooms: tub and shower descaled, toilet inside and out including the base, mirrors, fixtures polished
Dust top to bottom: ceiling fans, vents, door frames, baseboards, window sills, blinds
Floors: vacuum including edges and under furniture that can be moved, then mop
Beds made, trash out, a final walk-through of every room
Add-ons quoted separately: inside the oven, inside the fridge, inside windows, laundry.
Team timing
A two-person team on an average 3-bedroom, 2-bath home needs about four to five hours for a first clean and two and a half to three for a recurring one. Enter real
Team hours
: if first cleans keep running long, the price is wrong.
Writing the home notes
After the first visit, the team lead writes
Home notes
: where supplies and linens are, anything fragile, rooms to skip, and the client's preferences. The next team reads them before they knock.
Example

A family with a golden retriever and two kids books biweekly cleans. On the call the scheduler learns they have 4 bedrooms and 2.5 baths and want the guest bed changed every visit. The first deep clean takes the team five and a half hours; dog hair under the couches takes the most time. The team lead writes it all in the notes, and the next visit takes three hours.
Follow up
The office calls or texts the next day: "How did we do?" Put the score in
Client rating
. A 3 or below is a call from the owner the same day.
Clients rarely complain; they just cancel. Ratings and fast re-cleans catch problems before that happens.
Ratings after every clean
The day after each clean, the office asks for a score from 1 to 5 by text.
Put it in
Client rating
on the clean. The client card shows their average, and the Dashboard chart shows the average by team.
A 5: thank them, and ask for a review once in their first month.
A 4: ask what would have made it a 5, and add it to the home notes.
A 3 or lower: the owner or office manager calls within the day.
When a client is unhappy
Listen and write down exactly what was missed, room by room.
Offer a re-clean of those areas within 48 hours at no charge. Tick
Re-clean requested
on the original clean.
Send the same team if the client is happy with them, or the team lead's best pair if not.
Never argue about whether something was cleaned. Fix it, then learn from it.
Spot checks
The office manager or a team lead visits a few cleans each week, unannounced to the team but with the client's agreement.
Bathrooms: no hair in drains, no water spots on fixtures, toilet base clean
Kitchen: no crumbs on counter edges or in the sink drain, stovetop clean under the grates
Dust: tops of door frames, baseboards in corners, ceiling fan blades
Floors: edges vacuumed, no streaks after mopping
Home notes followed: the right products, the right rooms skipped
Learning from re-cleans

Look at the Re-cleans list monthly. If one area keeps coming up (baseboards, shower glass), make it a five-minute lesson at the next team meeting. If one team has most of them, the team lead and owner sit down with them.
Example

A move-out client gives a 3: the landlord found grease on the range hood. The office manager calls, apologizes, and books a re-clean of the kitchen the next morning. The re-clean is free; the client tells the landlord the deposit can be released. At the team meeting, range hoods are added to the move-out checklist.
Breakage
Accidents happen. The team lead tells the client the same day, takes a photo and writes it down. The owner decides on repair or replacement; it never comes out of a cleaner's pay.
Teams cannot clean well with an empty bottle. Each team's kit is checked weekly, and the shop shelf is counted every Friday.
What each team kit carries
All-purpose cleaner, glass cleaner, disinfectant, descaler and a stone-safe cleaner
A fragrance-free set for clients who need it
Microfiber cloths color-coded: blue for glass, green for kitchen, red for bathrooms, never mixed
Scrub pads, toothbrushes for grout, a squeegee, a duster with an extension pole
Vacuum with spare bags or a clean filter, a mop with fresh heads
Gloves, trash liners, shoe covers
The weekly count
Every Friday the office manager counts the shelf; team leads check their kits.
Type the count into
On hand
and set
Last counted
Anything showing
Reorder
goes on the order that day.
Laundering cloths and mop heads
Wash microfiber hot, without fabric softener, and air-dry or tumble low. Keep bathroom cloths in their own load. Replace cloths that stop picking up dust.
Mixing and safety
Never mix bleach with ammonia or acid cleaners.
Label every spray bottle with what is in it and the dilution.
Keep the safety sheets for every chemical in the van.
Supplies cost on each clean
Teams enter a rough supplies cost per clean (most run between 5 and 6 percent of the price). It makes the margin honest and shows when a team is using far more product than the others.
Example

On Friday Team B's kit is low on descaler and the shelf shows two bottles against a reorder point of four. The row flips to Reorder. The office orders a case on Friday afternoon and it arrives on Monday, before the three hard-water homes on Team B's Tuesday list.
Checklist when you run out on a job
Text the office before improvising with a client's products
Never use a client product on a surface you are not sure about
Write it on the clean so the kit is restocked
